blocks.text: Week 1 Kit: Latin Prefixes, Ten Verbs, and the gl- Family
This kit is for producing words, not recognizing them. The verb and light tables run from meaning to word, so cover the right-hand column and say the word.

Week 1 is the 20 prefixes, the gl- family and the first two verbs. The other eight verbs go two a week through week 5. A root is a tool for choosing a word and waking its image, never a rule about what the word must mean today.

The 20 prefixes and their disguises
A Latin prefix reshapes its last letter to match the next sound, so ad- turns up as ac-, af-, at- and plain a-. French wore many of these forms down further. Cover the Means column to test yourself.

rows: abduct (lead away); avert (turn away); abstain (hold away)
advance, advantage (ab + ante, "from before"; the d was added by mistake)
ad- (ac-, af-, ag-, al-, an-, ap-, ar-, as-, at-, a-)
accept (take to); attract (drag toward); aggravate (add weight to); aspire (breathe toward)
collide (strike together); cohere (stick together); corrupt (thoroughly broken)
companion (com + panis, "bread-sharer"); cost (con + stare, "stand at" a price); couch ("lay in place")
contradict (speak against); contrast (stand against); controversy (turned against)
country ("the land lying opposite"); counterfeit ("made against")
descend (climb down); depend (hang down); deciduous (falling off); devour (swallow down)
distract (drag apart); disrupt (break apart); digress (step apart); diffuse (pour apart)
dinner (dis + jejunare, "un-fast": the same idea as breakfast); dilapidated ("stones scattered")
expel (drive out); erupt (break out); elect (pick out); efface (wipe the face off)
escape (ex + cappa, "out of one's cape"); issue ("a going out"); astonish ("thunderstruck")
inject (throw in); invade (walk in); illuminate (light upon); irrigate (water in)
envy (in + videre, "look upon"); ambush ("into the woods"); employ ("fold in")
interrupt (break between); intervene (come between); intercept (seize between)
interval ("between the ramparts"); intelligent ("choosing between"); entertain ("hold between")
obstruct (build against); object (thrown in the way); occur (run to meet); offer (carry toward); omit (let go by)
obvious (ob + via, "in the road"); opportune ("toward the harbor")
perforate (bore through); permit (let through); perspire (breathe through); perfect (done through)
pilgrim (per + ager, "beyond the fields"); pardon ("give thoroughly")
predict (say before); prevent (come before); precise (cut off in front); president (sitting in front)
project (throw forward); promise (send forth); protect (cover in front); procrastinate (forward to tomorrow)
prose ("turned forward"); prudent (provident worn down, "seeing ahead"); purchase ("chase after"); portray ("draw forth")
repel (drive back); reflect (bend back); reluctant (struggling against); remorse (biting back); resilient (leaping back)
redundant (red + unda, "surging back like a wave"); ransom (redemption worn down); render ("give back")
seclude (shut apart); select (pick aside); seduce (lead aside); segregate (apart from the flock)
secure (se + cura, "apart from care"); sure (secure worn down); sever (separate worn down)
sub- (suc-, suf-, sug-, sum-, sup-, sur-, sus-)
subtract (drag from under); suffer (bear from under); suggest (carry up from under); suspend (hang up); surreptitious (snatched secretly)
supplant ("trip up by the sole of the foot"); souvenir ("come up from below" into mind); sudden ("coming up by stealth")
supervise (oversee); superfluous (overflowing); supercilious (over the eyelid: a raised eyebrow)
surround (super + unda, "overflow"; no relation to round); surreal ("above the real"); survive ("over-live"); sovereign; somersault ("over-leap")
transfer, translate (carry across); transparent (appearing through); transcend (climb across)
trance (trans + ire, "a going across"); tradition and treason (both "a handing over"); trespass ("pass across"); travesty ("cross-dress")

blocks.text: Two traps. The two in- prefixes are different words, which is why inflammable means "into flame." And a French sur- is almost always super-, not sub-: surface, survive, surround.
Surreal joins sur-, “above,” to real. Try it beside uncanny and dreamlike in a short description. Which one fits what the observer sees?
The first ten verbs

All ten are things a hand or body does: drag, hang, throw, send, seize, hold, turn, look, lead, carry. Every abstraction built on them has that movement inside it. Each family ends with one sentence where the image is awake; write your own for three words in each family.
1. trahere, tract-: to drag
Standing alone: tract (a stretch drawn out), traction, tractor ("puller").
Worn down: trace, train (what drags behind), trait (a stroke drawn), treat and treaty (a handling), retreat (a drawing back), portray and portrait (drawn forth), distraught (distracted, respelled).
Awake: He retracted the remark the way you haul in a net, hand over hand, with everything it had caught.
In the books:

rows: Ay, thou poor ghost, while memory holds a seat / In this distracted globe.
Globe is his head, the world and the theatre at once; distracted pulls all three apart.
Bradley leaned his elbows on his knees, and his head upon his hands, and looked at the fire with a most intent abstraction.
The body is placed exactly while the mind is dragged off; intent pulls the other way.

I vainly reminded him of his protracted abstinence from food: … if he stretched his hand out to get a piece of bread, his fingers clenched before they reached it, and remained on the table, forgetful of their aim.
E. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847), ch. XXXIV
The fast is drawn out over days; one hand that stops short of the bread shows it.
His guest turned on him a face pale as parchment in which two distraught eyes burned like great red letters.
Fitzgerald, "Tarquin of Cheapside", in Tales of the Jazz Age (1922)
Parchment and red letters turn the face into a written page; the eyes are pulled wide.

blocks.text: 2. pendere, pens-: to hang, to weigh, to pay
Romans once paid by weighing out metal on a hanging scale, so hang, weigh and pay are one verb.

rows: hanging straight, like a plumb line

blocks.text: Standing alone: pendant, pendulum, pending, pension (a payment).
Worn down: poise (weight), pound (by weight), spend (expend, worn down), pansy (French pensée, "thought"), penthouse (once pentis, a shed "hung on" a wall), penchant (a lean).
Expensive once carried the physical idea of weighing out payment. Imagine coins on a merchant’s scales.
Awake: She was pensive all through dinner, weighing each answer before she spent it.
In the books:

rows: …why the sepulchre / Wherein we saw thee quietly inurn'd, / Hath op'd his ponderous and marble jaws / To cast thee up again.
The tomb gets jaws. Ponderous gives them weight, then plain marble gives them stone.

She knew how to hit to a hair's-breadth that moment of evening when the light and the darkness are so evenly balanced that the constraint of day and the suspense of night neutralize each other, leaving absolute mental liberty.
Hardy, Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), ch. XIII
Evening as a pair of scales; suspense keeps its root, a weight left hanging.
…a profuse crop of hair impending over the top of his face, lending to his forehead the high- cornered outline of an early Gothic shield…
Hardy, The Return of the Native (1878), I.5
Impending in its root sense, hanging over. The usual sense, a threat, is left for the man.
He remained calm and silent, with his eyes fixed on the ground, and the tip of every finger of his right hand delicately poised against the tip of every finger of his left.
Poise is weighing: the fingertips balance like a scale while the man waits to speak.

blocks.text: 3. jacere, ject-: to throw
Worn down: jet, jetty (thrown out into the water), jettison, jetsam, jut.
A sister verb, jacēre, means "to lie," as a thrown thing lies: adjacent (lying near), gist ("it lies": where the case rests).
To project is to throw forward. A speaker can project her voice to the far end of a hall.
Awake: He sat dejected on the step, exactly as if someone had thrown him there.
In the books:

rows: Now entertain conjecture of a time / When creeping murmur and the poring dark / Fills the wide vessel of the universe.
Throw your guesses together, says the Chorus. Entertain, conjecture and universe are all kit words.
But he was restless; he ruffled up his hair and from time to time let his head drop into his hands dejectedly resting his ragged elbows on the stained and sticky table.
Dostoevsky, Crime and Punishment, tr. Constance Garnett (1914), I.2
The head is thrown down before the word arrives; dejectedly only names what we saw.
Mr. Bulstrode's sickly body, shattered by the agitations he had gone through since the last evening, made him feel abjectly in the power of this loud invulnerable man.
Abject means thrown away. The body does the throwing first; the feeling follows.

Across the roadway in the sunshine a short wooden pier jutted into the shallow pale water, which farther out had an intense blue tint contrasting unpleasantly with the green orderly slopes on the opposite shore.
Jut is jet worn down: a thing thrown out and left there.

blocks.text: 4. mittere, miss-: to send, to let go
Standing alone: mission, missile (a thing sent), missive, message.
Worn down: mess (a course "put" on the table, then the people sharing it, then a jumble), Mass (named for the dismissal at its end), demise (a sending away).
Awake: The rain was intermittent; the sky kept letting go and taking hold again.
In the books:

rows: …a spot where, by day, a fitful white streak of steam at intervals upon the dark green background denoted intermittent moments of contact between their secluded world and modern life.
Hardy, Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), ch. XXX
A train seen only as steam, sent out and let go. Secluded, shut away, answers it.
"Captain Mayhew, stand by now to receive it"; and taking the fatal missive from Starbuck's hands, he caught it in the slit of the pole, and reached it over towards the boat.
A letter literally sent: carried out over the water on the end of a pole.

Her shoulders felt the warmth of the rock; now and then a whiff of cooler air seemed to slip down upon her head from above; the ravine at her feet, choked full of vegetation, emitted the faint, drowsy hum of insect life.
Emit sends something out of a place, so the whole ravine becomes the speaker.
On this reputation, and on the broken heart of Mr Pipchin, she had contrived, taking one year with another, to eke out a tolerable sufficient living since her husband's demise.
Demise, a sending away, is the lawyer's word for a death. Its coldness makes the joke.

blocks.text: 5. capere, capt-: to take, to seize
In compounds the stem becomes -cip- and -cept-; French turned it into -ceive.

rows: take hold of an idea, or a child
a taking in hand, a start

blocks.text: Standing alone: capture, captive, capable (able to hold), capacity.
Worn down: catch and chase (one word in two dialects of French), purchase ("chase after"), cable (a lasso), case and cash (a box that holds).
English cousins from the same ancient root: have, heave, heavy.
Awake: She tried to conceive of the distance, but her mind closed on it and came away empty, like a hand on water.
In the books:

rows: 'Twas pretty, though a plague, / To see him every hour; to sit and draw / His arched brows, his hawking eye, his curls, / In our heart's table—heart too capable / Of every line and trick of his sweet favour.
Shakespeare, All's Well That Ends Well 1.1
Capable means able to take in. The heart is a drawing board that keeps every line.
As the captive men were faded and haggard, so the iron was rusty, the stone was slimy, the wood was rotten, the air was faint, the light was dim.
One captive, then five short clauses: the prison takes on the state of its prisoners.
They floated in his mind agreeably enough, and as he took up his bed- candle his lips were curled with that incipient smile which is apt to accompany agreeable recollections.
Incipient, just taking hold: the moment before a smile is quite a smile.

…and eyes, had they been agreeable in expression, that would have been irresistible: fortunately for my susceptible heart, the only sentiment they evinced hovered between scorn and a kind of desperation, singularly unnatural to be detected there.
E. Brontë, Wuthering Heights (1847), ch. II
Lockwood's vanity in one word: a heart that takes impressions too easily.

blocks.text: 6. tenere, tent-: to hold
In compounds the stem becomes -tin- and -tain.
Standing alone: tenant (a holder), tenure, tenet ("he holds"), tenable, tenacious, tenor (the voice that held the melody).
Worn down: countenance (how you hold yourself, then your face), rein (from retain: a holding back).
False friends: tend, tense, extend and attend come from tendere, "to stretch"; attain comes from tangere, "to touch."
Awake: Her countenance held. It was the last thing in the room she still had a grip on.
In the books:

rows: A beardless, boyish face, very fair, no features to speak of, nose peeling, little blue eyes, smiles and frowns chasing each other over that open countenance like sunshine and shadow on a wind-swept plain.
Conrad, Heart of Darkness (1899), pt. II
Countenance is how a face is held. Here nothing holds, and weather crosses it.
His lips meantime sustained his precious cigar, that (for him) first necessary and prime luxury of life; its blue wreaths curled prettily enough amongst the flowers, and in the evening light.
Sustain at its root, to hold up from below. The large word on a small job is the joke.

This parlour looked gloomy: a neglected handful of fire burnt low in the grate; and, leaning over it, with his head supported against the high, old-fashioned mantelpiece, appeared the blind tenant of the room.
C. Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847), ch. XXXVII
The sentence makes us wait for the man. Tenant says he holds the room, and little else.
So he locked up the Bower and they set forth: Mr Venus taking his arm, and keeping it with remarkable tenacity.
Tenacity made literal: one man will not let go of another's arm.
Here be it said, that this pertinacious pursuit of one particular whale, continued through day into night, and through night into day, is a thing by no means unprecedented in the South sea fishery.
Holding on thoroughly. Day into night, night into day: the phrase turns back on itself like the chase.

blocks.text: 7. vertere, vers-: to turn
Standing alone: verse (a turn, like a plow's at the end of a furrow), version, versatile, vertigo (a whirling), vertebra (a joint to turn on), vortex, versus.
Verse turns back at the end of each line and prose goes straight on. The two words say exactly that.
English cousins from the same ancient root: -ward (toward, inward), warp, weird (Old English wyrd, "fate": how things turn out), and the wr- words wring, wrist, writhe, wry.
Warp names a change of shape. Compare a board that warps in damp air with a reflection that bends in moving water.
Awake: On the anniversary the year turned over in its sleep and showed the same face.
In the books:

rows: The heroic follower of Garibaldi, at the thought of the eternal stillness and silence fallen upon the shrouded form stretched out on the bed upstairs, averted his face and raised his hand to his furrowed brow.
Averting is turning away. The long clause before it delays the turn the way grief does.
Her eyes, which were grey with a shade of green through them, had a habit of glancing upwards when she spoke with anyone, which made her look like a little perverse madonna.
Perverse, turned the wrong way, set against madonna. The upturned eyes do both.
They stooped in a long curve down into the golden glow, concentrating, cawing, wheeling, like black flakes on a slow vortex, over a tree clump that made a dark boss among the pasture.
Three participles wheel before the noun names the turning.
Her fair face was stained to a warm olive glow and on her arms and the half moon of her back writhed painted serpents with single eyes of venomous green.
Fitzgerald, "The Camel's Back", in Tales of the Jazz Age (1922)
Writhe is an English cousin of vertere. The verb comes before its subject, so the twisting is seen before the snakes.

blocks.text: 8. specere, spect-: to look
In compounds the stem becomes -spic-.

rows: how a thing looks from one side

blocks.text: Standing alone: spectacle, spectator, specter (an appearance), spectrum, specimen, species (a look, then a kind), special, specious (good-looking, then only good-looking), speculate (to watch from a tower).
Worn down: spice (species, "kinds of goods"), despite and spite (a looking down on), respite (respect, respelled: a looking back, then a delay granted), spy.
Greek cousins, with the sounds swapped: scope, telescope, skeptic, bishop (epi + skopos, "overseer").
Awake: He respected her; even walking away he kept looking back.
In the books:

rows: Thy bones are marrowless, thy blood is cold; / Thou hast no speculation in those eyes / Which thou dost glare with.
Speculation is the power of looking. The ghost glares and cannot see.
So all ere day-spring, under conscious night, / Secret they finished, and in order set, / With silent circumspection, unespied.
Looking all around, then unespied: one root gives both the watcher and the unwatched.
The table was set for company in the dining-room, where highly varnished wood and colored glass and useless pieces of china were conspicuous enough to satisfy the standards of the new prosperity.
Conspicuous means made to be seen. The word does the judging, so the narrator need not.
…only it rose, it sank, it rolled continuously, without respite and rest, like a rock that should have miraculously struck adrift from a coast and gone wallowing upon the sea.
Respite is a pause granted. The three short verbs before it refuse one.

blocks.text: 9. ducere, duct-: to lead

rows: lead back (a doctor still reduces a dislocated shoulder)
lead across as a spectacle, and so slander

blocks.text: Standing alone: duct, ductile (able to be drawn out), duke (a leader), aqueduct, viaduct.
Worn down: conduit, doge, redoubt (a place to be led back to: a retreat).
English cousins from the same ancient root: tug, tow, team (animals that pull together).
Awake: Nobody pushed him. He was seduced: led aside one polite step at a time, until the road was out of sight.
In the books:

rows: How now? a conduit, girl? What, still in tears? / Evermore show'ring?
A conduit leads water. Capulet turns his weeping daughter into a fountain pipe.
His tenderness had rendered him ductile in a priest's hands…
Ductile metal can be drawn into wire; a good man is drawn out by a priest.
Upon its head, with red extended mouth and solitary eye of fire, sat the hideous beast whose craft had seduced me into murder, and whose informing voice had consigned me to the hangman.
Seduce means to lead aside. The murderer hands the leading over to the cat.
The sexton-task of piling earth above John Harmon all night long, was not conducive to sound sleep…
An office word set beside a grave. The understatement does the work.

blocks.text: 10. ferre, lat-: to carry, to bear
The verb borrowed its second stem from another verb, so each fer- word has a lat- twin. Transfer and translate are one verb.
Standing alone: fertile (bearing), conifer (cone-bearer), Lucifer (light-bearer).
English cousins from the same ancient root: bear, birth, burden, bier, barrow.
Greek cousins: metaphor ("carry across," the twin of transfer and translate), periphery (the twin of circumference), phosphorus (the twin of Lucifer), euphoria.
False friends: ferry is unrelated; dilate and latitude come from latus, "wide."
Awake: He translated the letter, carrying each sentence across the gap and losing a little on every trip.
In the books:

rows: Bless thee, Bottom, bless thee! Thou art translated.
Translated in its root sense, carried across. Bottom now has an ass's head.
Suffer the little children to come unto me, and forbid them not: for of such is the kingdom of God.
Suffer in its old sense, to bear and so to allow.
I have met him coming out of her presence with a mischievous half-smile about his lips, and in his eyes a look as of masculine vanity elate and tickled.
Elate means carried up. One Latin word and one English word, both lifting.
Dorothea wondered a little, but felt that it would be indelicate just then to ask for any information which Mr. Casaubon did not proffer, and she turned to the window to admire the view.
Proffer means to carry forward and hold out. What Casaubon withholds becomes the story.

blocks.text: The gl- family: words for light
These thirteen words for light all begin with gl-, and most descend from one root meaning "to shine," the same root as gold, yellow and glad. Glad first meant "bright."

rows: steady light from inside a thing, warm, no flame
embers, a lampshade, a phone under a blanket
soft steady shine off something smooth, or a thin ray in the dark
polished wood, an eye, light under a door
strong, harsh light that hurts to look at
sun on a windshield, a bare bulb
faint light that wavers at the edge of seeing
a far candle, a porch light through trees
one small hard flash off a point or edge
a ring, a blade, a pair of glasses
frost, sequins, broken glass on a road
the shine of something wet or oiled
dew, sweat, a fish, an eye about to spill
the even shine of a smooth surface
a glassy coat; of eyes, a film
ice on a branch, a bored stare
light striking and sliding off; a quick look
a blow sliding off armor, eyes meeting and leaving
a brief, partial view (at first, a flash)
a face in a passing train
the hour when daylight fades into evening
an old form of glitter, kept by poets

blocks.text: The endings tell you how the light behaves. Every unsteady light carries -er or -le, the endings that mean "again and again": glimmer, glitter, shimmer, flicker, sparkle, twinkle. The steady ones carry neither: glow, gleam, glare, shine.

rows: glow, gleam, glare, gloss; shine, sheen, blaze

blocks.text: Five neighbors worth separating:
shimmer: soft wavering light over a surface (heat, silk, water)
flicker: quick, irregular on-and-off (a candle, a failing tube)
sparkle: lively small flashes, warmer than glitter (water in sun, a gem)
twinkle: a small far point going on and off (stars)
sheen: a soft shine lying on a surface (satin, a horse's coat, oil on water)
A brass button can glimmer in a dark cupboard; a curtain of rain can shimmer. If a reflection changes shape as it moves, try warp.
Drill: write one sentence for each of six words, so that swapping in a neighbor would make it false.
Sources

The twelve most surprising derivations were checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary on the as-of date: surround, trance, prose, gist, mess, penthouse, countenance, respite, glad, weird, dinner, spice.
The rest are the standard derivations, given from memory. Look up any you plan to rely on in print.

The sentences in every "In the books" table, here and in weeks 6 to 20, are quoted from public-domain texts. Those texts are Project Gutenberg editions read through the GITenberg mirror, the ELTeC collection of English novels and the NLTK copy of the Gutenberg corpus. Each sentence was checked letter for letter against them after it went into the doc. Only books first published before 1929, or translations published by then, are quoted. Chapter numbers follow those editions; a print edition may number them differently.
Week 2: Sound, and the Room

Week 2 is verbs 3 and 4 (throw, send), the cl- and cr- families for sound, and thirty-two names from your own room. Start each session by covering the right-hand columns of the Week 1 tables and saying the words.
Verbs 3 and 4: throw and send
The full families are in the first tab under jacere and mittere. Learn those, then decode these nine from prefix and root before you look right.

rows: things thrown out, as by a volcano
the state of being cast down
send from the hand: free a slave
the things "sent before," named earlier in a deed: the property

blocks.text: Awake drill: write one sentence each for jettison, dismiss and intermittent in which something is physically thrown or let go.
The cl- and cr- families: words for sound
English often groups hard sounds by their first letters: cl- for things striking, cr- for things breaking or straining. Compare roar, click, whoosh, jingle, clatter, twitter, blare and bark.

rows: one small sharp tick of a mechanism
a latch, a pen, a light switch
a flat hard knock of wood or plastic
a car door, a washing machine
a small high ring of glass or thin metal
a dull knock of heavy metal, with no ring
chains, a radiator, tools in a bag
one loud ringing blow on metal
a gate, a bell, a dropped pan lid
a run of loose hard knocks
a branch, a whip, ice on a lake
a long thin complaint of strained wood or metal
a stair, a hinge, a rope under load
a loud collapse of many hard things
a shelf of dishes, a breaking wave
a frog, a throat after sleep

blocks.text: The vowel tells you the size. English leans on i for small, high sounds and on a, o and u for bigger, lower ones.
The endings -le and -er mean repetition here too: rattle, rustle, jingle, tinkle, crackle, sizzle, gurgle; clatter, patter, chatter, mutter, sputter, twitter.

rows: click, clack, clunk, knock, rap, thud, thump
clang, clink, chime, peal, toll, jingle, tinkle
hiss, swish, whoosh, rustle, sigh, whisper, wheeze
hum, drone, rumble, purr, murmur, thrum
wail, whine, howl, shriek, screech, squeal, groan

blocks.text: Drill: sit beside an open window for ten minutes. Give each sound one exact word. Describe a window covering, the frame and an animal outside without using jingle, roar or bark.
Inventory: the room
Learn thirty-two names for parts of a window, blinds and a bed. Cover the right-hand column and identify each part on a real object.
The window:

rows: the fixed surround set into the wall
the panel that holds the glass; in some windows it slides
the ledge at the bottom of the frame
either upright side of the frame
the beam in the wall above the opening
the channel the sash slides in
an upright edge-piece of a sash
the top or bottom edge-piece of a sash
the two stiles that overlap when the window is shut
a thin bar dividing one sash into panes
a post between two windows set side by side
the catch that locks the sash
the small slot that drains rain out of the track
the trim around the window on the wall
the trim board under the sill, indoors
the thickness of wall you see beside the frame

blocks.text: The blinds:

rows: the weighted bar at the bottom
the strings that hold the slats like rungs
the rod you twist to tilt the slats
the string that raises the whole blind

blocks.text: The bed:

rows: the tough cloth, often striped, that cases a mattress or pillow
the soft under-feathers of a duck or goose
the stiff shaft of a feather, the part that pokes through
the fabric walls inside a duvet that keep the down from sliding
how high and springy the filling stands
a strip sewn into a pillow's side to give it depth
the corded ridge along a seam
the finished edge of woven cloth, which won't fray

blocks.text: Loft is the height and spring of the filling in a pillow or quilt.
Drill: coin three two-word names for familiar things in a room that have no everyday name.
The definitions in this tab are standard ones, given from memory. Look up any you plan to rely on in print.
Week 3: Movement, and the Street
Week 3 is verbs 5 and 6 (seize, hold), three families for movement, and thirty-one names from a street. Start each session with last week's sound table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 5 and 6: seize and hold
The full families are in the first tab under capere and tenere. Learn those, then decode these ten from prefix and root before you look right.

rows: a thing conceived: a fancy, then vanity
out of the hand's grasp: set free
those retained: a great person's followers
the tongue of wood that holds a joint together
not pertaining, and so out of place, then rude
what holds you up from below: food

blocks.text: Awake drill: write one sentence each for perceive, obtain and tenacious in which a hand actually closes on something.
fl-, sl- and sw-: words for movement
Three English families sort movement by its feel: fl- is quick and free, sl- is smooth, low or slack, and sw- travels in an arc. Slide belongs to the second group.

rows: darts lightly from place to place
a moth, a wren, a glance
beats fast and small, as a thin thing does
a flag, eyelids, a moth at a bulb
a tarp, a crow, a loose sole
comes and goes quickly and unsteadily
the arms of a swimmer in trouble
is thrown with a loose sudden swing
draws back sharply from pain or fear
a hand from a hot pan
a fish on a deck, a body into a chair
moves over a surface without leaving it
a drawer, a sash, a foot on ice
slides by accident, losing its hold
a heel, a knot, a wet plate
slides with a winding, belly-down motion
a snake, a stocking off a chair
moves low and quiet to avoid notice
sits or stands with the back let go
a bored student, a hat brim
a body, a roof under snow
moves sloppily in or with liquid
water in a bucket, boots in mud
moves slowly side to side from a fixed base
trees, a rope bridge, a drunk
moves back and forth from a fixed point above
a gate, a hanging lamp, a leg
turns aside suddenly from a straight course
comes down fast in a curve
moves in one clean wide curve over a surface

Week 6: Touch, and the Cloth

Week 6 is verbs 11 and 12 (touch, press), three English families for contact, a palette for texture, and thirty names from the cloth on your bed. The first ten verbs are finished, so from here each week's two verbs get their full families in the weekly tab. Start each session with last week's smell table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 11 and 12: touch and press

The second ten verbs work like the first ten: each is a plain act, and every abstraction built on it keeps the act inside. This week's two are what a fingertip does and what a palm does. Read the left column, cover the right, and say the word.
11. tangere, tact-: to touch
In compounds the stem thins to -ting- and -tig-. An older form, tag-, hides in integer and contagion.

rows: a touching that passes something on
touching on; so, depending on what it touches
touching: a line that meets a curve at one point and goes on
of touch; a light touch with people

blocks.text: Standing alone: tact, tactile, tangent, tangible.

Worn down: entire (integer through French), tax (probably "to touch again and again", so to handle and to value), task (tax with two sounds swapped), taste (apparently the same handling verb; it first meant to feel, pat or stroke).
False friend: tang and tangy are not in this family. Tang is Scandinavian, and in English it first meant a snake's tongue; it waits in week 7.
Awake: He kept one room of the house intact, in the strict sense: nobody had touched it since she left.
In the books:

rows: 'Tis now the very witching time of night, / When churchyards yawn, and hell itself breathes out / Contagion to this world.
A touching that passes something on, breathed out like air.
Nothing moved in sky, land, or sea, except a frill of milkwhite foam along the nearer angles of the shore, shreds of which licked the contiguous stones like tongues.
Hardy, Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), ch. XLVII
Contiguous means touching along an edge. Licked like tongues makes the touch literal.
And if Brangwen's heart had not been hard and intact with anger, like a precious stone, he would have agreed.
Untouched, and so whole. The precious stone makes it something you could hold.
Far into the night she sat alone, by the sinking blaze, in dark and threatening beauty, watching the murky shadows looming on the wall, as if her thoughts were tangible, and cast them there.
Thoughts made touchable, then cast as shadows: Edith's mind on the wall.
…shall we now / Contaminate our fingers with base bribes / And sell the mighty space of our large honors / For so much trash as may be grasped thus?
Touched, and so spoiled, set on the fingers that do the touching; grasped closes it.

blocks.text: 12. premere, press-: to press
Almost every compound keeps press-. The other stem, prem-, thins to -prim- and survives in reprimand.

rows: a thing to be pressed back

blocks.text: Standing alone: press, pressure.
Worn down: print (a thing pressed), and so imprint, footprint and fingerprint. A thumb pressed into soft clay makes an imprint.

False friends: press-gang and "pressed into service" come from an older word, prest, which goes back to praestare, "to stand before". That verb is week 10's. Impresario and enterprise come from prehendere, to seize.
Awake: The day left its impression on him the way a head leaves one on a pillow: a dent that takes hours to fill.
In the books:

rows: What a piece of work is a man! how noble in reason! how infinite in faculties! in form and moving how express and admirable!
Express as an adjective: pressed out, exact, like a coin struck from a die.
The sense of the heavy, brooding silence in the outside world seemed to enter and fill the room— the oppressive infinity of it, without breath, without light.
Oppressive keeps its weight. Silence presses down, and the two withouts take the air away.

Depressed and slinking though they were, eyes of fire were not wanting among them; nor compressed lips, white with what they suppressed; nor foreheads knitted into the likeness of the gallows-rope they mused about enduring, or inflicting.
Dickens, A Tale of Two Cities (1859), I.5
Three press words in one sentence: depressed, compressed, suppressed. The lips go white from pressing.
…with the hard glazed hat in his one hand, and a red equator round his head which it had newly imprinted there.
The hat has pressed a line round Captain Cuttle's head; equator makes the head a globe.

Week 7: Taste, and the Mouth

Week 7 is verbs 13 and 14 (cut, break), the English words for eating and drinking, a palette for taste, and thirty names from the mouth and the table. Start each session with last week's texture table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 13 and 14: cut and break
This week's two verbs are what a mouth does to food: teeth cut, jaws break. Both made large families, and both hide in short English words that look native.
13. caedere, caes-: to cut, to strike down
In compounds caed- becomes -cid- and caes- becomes -cis-: decide, decision.

cut off in front, cut short
a cut: the pause inside a line of verse

blocks.text: Worn down: chisel (a cutting tool), cement (first, the stone chips cut for mortar), scissors.
Scissors comes from caedere, but its sc- is borrowed. In the 1500s it was respelled after Latin scissor, a tailor, which belongs to a different verb: scindere, to split.

Sister verb: secare, sect-, to cut. It gives section, sector, segment, dissect, bisect, intersect and insect ("cut into": the notched body). English saw and scythe are its cousins, and scythe probably picked up the same false sc-.
Awake: He decided the way a butcher does, in one stroke, and did not look at what fell away.
In the books:

rows: Lord Angelo is precise; / Stands at a guard with envy; scarce confesses / That his blood flows, or that his appetite / Is more to bread than stone.
Precise first meant cut short. Angelo is a man trimmed down until he is nearly stone.
Near him, her black form merged in the night, like a figure half chiselled out of a block of black stone.
Conrad, The Secret Agent (1907), ch. XII
Half chiselled: Winnie Verloc is still part of the dark she is cut from.
Let's purge this choler without letting blood— / This we prescribe, though no physician; / Deep malice makes too deep incision.
The king talks like a surgeon. Incision and prescribe, a cut and a writing, sit two lines apart.
The sun arose with a sickly yellow lustre, and clambered a very few degrees above the horizon—emitting no decisive light.
Decisive means cutting, and this light cuts nothing. Emitting is week 1's mittere.

blocks.text: Worn down: frail (fragile through French; the two are one word) and refrain, the line where a song breaks off and comes back.
Cousins: break and breach are traced to the same ancient root.

Sister verb: rumpere, rupt-, to burst. You have erupt, interrupt, disrupt and corrupt from week 1's prefixes; rupture and abrupt are the plain ones. Worn down, it gives bankrupt (Italian for "broken bench"), route (a road forced through) and rout (a troop broken up).
A strip of colored glass can distort a straight line. Refract refers to the bending of a light ray; warp describes the altered shape you see.

rows: Frail and fragile are one word. The line speaks to breakability as if it were a person.
These fragments I have shored against my ruins

His face was kind and he joined gently the fingers of each hand, forming a frail cage by the union of their tips.
Joyce, A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man (1916), ch. 3

…at any rate he glanced at the refractory arm, at Pierre's terror-stricken face, and again at the arm, and on his face a feeble, piteous smile appeared…

Week 8: Weather, and the Sky

Week 8 is verbs 15 and 16 (fall, pour), the English families for water coming down, two scales for rain and wind, and thirty names from the sky over your street. Start each session with last week's taste table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 15 and 16: fall and pour
Weather is two motions, things falling and things pouring. Latin built its words for luck out of the first and its words for mixing out of the second.
15. cadere, cas-: to fall
In compounds cad- becomes -cid-: accident. Last week's caedere also gives -cid-, so ask the sense: does something fall, or get cut?

rows: a thing that befalls; then the one it befalls
a falling toward: the moment things fall your way
what falls in along the way
to fall on the same spot together
the fall of a voice or a line
where the sun falls: the west

blocks.text: Worn down: chance (how the dice fall), chute (a fall), cheat.
Cheat is escheat cut short: property that "fell" to a lord. The sense slid from confiscate to deceive. Chance and cadence are one word, cadentia, worn two ways.
The other case, a box, is a different word. It comes from capere, verb 5.
Awake: It was an accident in the old sense: it fell on them, like weather.
In the books:

rows: How all occasions do inform against me / And spur my dull revenge!
Occasions are what falls out. Everything that happens becomes a witness against him.
Wherein I spake of most disastrous chances, / Of moving accidents by flood and field, / Of hair-breadth 'scapes i' the imminent deadly breach…
Accidents are what befalls, and chances is the same root worn down: two cadere words in two lines.
Her figure slightly bent, her hand well up, and her right arm stretched out, she gave herself up to the cadence of the movement that rocked her in her saddle.
Flaubert, Madame Bovary, tr. Eleanor Marx- Aveling (1886), II.9
Cadence is a falling, then a rhythm of falls. Emma gives herself up to it, and the sentence rocks.
The black wraith of a deciduous creeper flapped from the porch, and the thin wooden walls, under their worn coat of paint, seemed to shiver in the wind that had risen with the ceasing of the snow.
Deciduous, falling off: the creeper has dropped its leaves, and only a wraith is left.

blocks.text: 16. fundere, fus-: to pour, to melt
The stem is steady: -fund- in the present, -fus- in the past.

Worn down: found and foundry (to pour metal), font (a casting of type), fondue ("melted"), funnel (what you pour in through), confound (confuse through French), refuse (refund's twin: to pour back what is offered).
Cousins: the dictionary traces gust, gush, gut and geyser to the same ancient root for pouring, with some doubt. If it holds, a gust of wind is a pour of air.

Sister verb: fluere, flux-, to flow. It gives fluid, fluent, flux, influx, affluent ("flowing toward"), confluence, fluctuate ("move in waves") and mellifluous ("flowing with honey"). Influence first meant a flowing-in from the stars, and influenza is the same word in Italian.
Awake: By evening the two stories were confused: poured into one glass, and nobody could pour them apart.
In the books:

rows: Confusion now hath made his masterpiece.
Confusion, a pouring together, made into a person. The murderer is never named.
Bird thou never wert, / That from Heaven, or near it, / Pourest thy full heart / In profuse strains of unpremeditated art.
Pourest, then profuse: the English verb and the Latin adjective say the same thing.
…green against a blue sky that was suffused with dust colour on the horizon.
Suffused, poured from beneath: colour rising into the sky from the earth's edge.

Week 9: Voice, and the Dog

Week 9 is verbs 17 and 18 (say, call), three English families for ways of speaking, a scale for how loud a voice is, and thirty names for parts of a dog. Start each session with last week's water table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 17 and 18: say and call
Latin split speech into two acts: dicere, to say a thing, and vocare, to call to someone. English built its words for law on the first and its words for summoning on the second.
17. dicere, dict-: to say
The root behind it meant "to show, to point out", and a second form, dicare, meant "to proclaim". Both senses survive in the family.

Cousins: teach first meant "to show", and token is a sign; both are traced to the same ancient root. So are digit, the pointing finger, and Greek paradigm, "shown beside".

Verbs 19 and 20: stand and sit
The last two verbs are the ones for staying put, and they are the largest families in the kit. Latin made its words for being, lasting and owning out of standing and sitting.
19. stare, stat-: to stand
Stare gives -stant, -stance and -stit-. Its partner sistere, to make stand, gives every -sist.
