The glosses in the two verb tables, the note on thorough and mantel, and the house names are standard, given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.
Week 12: Running, and the Bus

Week 12 pairs verbs 23 and 24 (run and come) with the sk- family for quick, light motion, a scale for the way vehicles move, and thirty names for parts of a bus. Begin each session by covering the right-hand column of last week’s edges table and recalling the words.
Verbs 23 and 24: run and come
These two are the verbs of travel: one runs, the other arrives. Both hide in plain words you would never suspect, including the word inventory.
23. currere, curs-: to run

rows: what runs from hand to hand
a running to and fro, of talk
to run up under, to help
a racecourse; then a course of study

blocks.text: Worn down: course, courier (a runner), corridor (a running place), corsair (one who runs raids), and career, which first meant a racecourse.
Cousins: car, carry, cargo, charge and chariot. They come from a Gaulish word for a wagon that Latin borrowed, and the dictionary traces it to the same root for running.
Awake: His career was a career in the old sense: a run at full speed down a track somebody else had laid.
In the books:

rows: (O God! a beast that wants discourse of reason / Would have mourn'd longer)
Discourse, a running to and fro: reason that moves from one thought to the next.
Shall quips and sentences and these paper bullets of the brain awe a man from the career of his humour?
Career in the old sense, a gallop down the lists. Benedick will not be talked out of his charge.

Morning, noon, and night, morning, noon, and night, each recurring with its accompanying monotony, always the same reluctant return of the same sequences of machinery, like a dragging piece of clockwork.
Recur, to run back. The sentence repeats its opening so the reader runs back too.
After a cursory inspection of the pillow-cases, leather pennants, and Gibson Girls that lined the walls, he left, and continued along Nassau Street with his hands in his pockets.
Fitzgerald, This Side of Paradise (1920), I.2
Cursory, run over quickly. The list is the inspection.
…To bogs and mires, and oft through pond or pool; / There swallowed up and lost, from succour far.
Succour, running up from below to help. Far puts the help out of reach.

blocks.text: 24. venire, vent-: to come

rows: a list of what was found
to come before, and so to stop
to come around, to get past

blocks.text: Worn down: souvenir, from week 1: what comes up from below, into the mind.
Cousin: come itself is traced to the same ancient root.
Every inventory in this kit is a venire word: a list of what you came upon.
Awake: She invented nothing. She came upon it, the way you come upon a coin in a coat.
In the books:

rows: It shall be inventoried, and every particle and utensil labell'd to my will: as—item, two lips indifferent red; item, two grey eyes with lids to them; item, one neck, one chin, and so forth.
Olivia mocks the love poet's list. An inventory is what you come upon, so she lists her face like furniture.
I prevented the dawning of the morning, and cried: I hoped in thy word.
Prevent in its root sense, to come before: he was up before the dawn.
The rose will redden in the bog, / The aster on the hill / Her everlasting fashion set, / And covenant gentians frill…
Covenant, a coming together, used as an adjective: the gentians keep an agreement with the season.
The parvenu, who had been induced by my artifices in the early part of the evening, to drink deeply, now shuffled, dealt, or played, with a wild nervousness of manner…
Parvenu, one who has just arrived. The newcomer at the card table is the easy mark.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take occur, cursory, event and convenient. Use each so that something runs or arrives.
Quick, light motion: the sk- family
English keeps its quick, light, low movements under one sound, spelled sk or sc. Week 3 gave you scurry; here is the rest of the family.

rows: a stone on water, a hand over a rail
a child, a needle on a record
runs lightly, with quick small steps
runs low and fast for cover
is driven fast before the wind
climbs in a rush, on hands and feet

blocks.text: How a vehicle moves
Which verb would a standing passenger use for the movement of a bus? The first row runs from the slowest movement to the wildest. The second row describes what happens when a ride goes wrong.

rows: idle, creep, crawl, roll, coast, cruise, rumble, barrel, hurtle, careen
lurch, jolt, judder, swerve, skid, fishtail, stall

blocks.text: A bus also sounds. It idles, hisses at the brakes, wheezes at the doors, rattles and whines. Those are week 2's words, put to work.
Drill: write the bus arriving and leaving in six verbs, three from each row.
Inventory: the bus
Follow a passenger from the stop to a seat. The thirty names below follow what they can touch and see, starting outside, moving inside and ending with the working parts.
Outside

rows: the lit sign that names the route
the mirror on an arm beside the driver
the hollow a wheel sits in
the cap over a wheel's center
the bar across the front or the back
the flap that hangs behind a wheel
the pipe the exhaust leaves by

blocks.text: Inside

rows: the box the fare drops into
a bar to hold, along a seat or the ceiling
a loop that hangs for standing riders
the cord you pull to ask for a stop
a seat for two or three, with no divider
the line standing riders must stay behind
the escape door in the ceiling

blocks.text: The works

rows: the panel of dials in front of the driver
the dial that counts the miles
the brake that works by compressed air, and hisses
the springs that carry the body over the wheels
the flashing light that says which way
the red light at the back
the grille of pipes that cools the engine

blocks.text: Give a bus one smell, then locate a passenger by naming three parts: what supports their weight, what their hand grips and what they can see when they look up.
Drill: ride a bus this week, or remember one. Write eight sentences, each with one name, in the order a rider meets them.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots kers- and gwa-, which list every word in the two verb tables, the car cousins, inventory and come.
The glosses, the note on career, and the bus names are standard, given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.
Week 13: Leaping, and the Land

Week 13 is verbs 25 and 26 (leap, climb), the j- family for sudden motion, a scale for slopes, and thirty names from the land outside the bus window. Start each session with last week's vehicle scale, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 25 and 26: leap and climb
These are the verbs for leaving the ground: one jumps, the other goes up rung by rung. Latin made its words for attack and for scorn out of the jump.
25. salire, salt-: to leap
In compounds the stem thins to -sil- and -sult-: resilient, insult.

rows: to spring back, as a consequence
leaping from one thing to another
a leap out from a besieged place

blocks.text: Insult kept its violence for a while: in English it first meant to triumph over someone arrogantly. A desultor was a circus rider who jumped from one galloping horse to another.
Awake: The talk was desultory in the circus sense: it leapt from horse to horse and rode none of them home.
In the books:

rows: I, as I said, was sitting in the deep chair, Leonora was standing in the window twirling the wooden acorn at the end of the window-blind cord desultorily round and round.
Desultory first meant a circus rider leaping from horse to horse. Here it is a hand that cannot settle.
…where crime has been committed, and shall exult to behold the whole earth one stain of guilt, one mighty blood spot.
Exult, to leap out. The devil's sermon leaps from single places to the whole earth.
The sound was curiously flawed by the wind; and I was listening, and thinking how the wind assailed and tore it, when I heard a footstep on the stair.
Assail, to leap upon. The wind attacks the sound of the bells, and then comes the footstep that changes Pip's life.
Where the high light fell, Jukes could see the salient ribs of one, the yellow, wistful face of another; bowed necks; or would meet a dull stare directed at his face.
Salient, leaping out: the ribs jump forward in the lamplight.

blocks.text: 26. scandere, scans-: to climb
In compounds the stem becomes -scend-.

rows: to climb down with someone: to stoop
to climb a verse, foot by foot
to go up by ladders; to step up

blocks.text: The scale of a fish and the scale that weighs are two other words. Greek has a cousin, scandal: first a trap that springs, then a stumbling block. Slander is scandal worn down through French.
Awake: He condescended to her: climbed down, rung by rung, so that she could watch him doing it.
In the books:

rows: …he had never in his life witnessed such behaviour in a person of rank—such affability and condescension, as he had himself experienced from Lady Catherine.
Condescend, to climb down. Mr Collins praises it, and the praise exposes him.
Gradually she realized that the night was common and ordinary, that the great, blistering, transcendent night did not really exist.
Transcend, to climb across and beyond. Three adjectives build the night up so the sentence can take it down.
A high, clear flame, an immense and lonely flame, ascended from the ocean, and from its summit the black smoke poured continuously at the sky.
Ascend, to climb up; summit finishes the climb.
Among the field guns on the brow of the hill the general in command of the rearguard stood with a staff officer, scanning the country through his fieldglass.
Tolstoy, War and Peace, tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude (1922), II.6
Scan, to climb: the eye goes over the country step by step, as a reader goes over a line of verse.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take salient, result, transcend and scale. Use each so that something leaves the ground.
Sudden motion: the j- family
English gives its abrupt movements a j, a sound that starts with a stop. Each word below is one sharp event.

rows: a sharp pull that stops short
a hard sudden knock or shake
a light push; a slow bouncing run
a heavy bounce on a seat
a truck on a dirt road

blocks.text: Two scales: the bounce and the slope

rows: bob, hop, skip, bounce, spring, bound, leap, vault
level, gentle, rolling, sloping, steep, sheer, precipitous, overhanging

blocks.text: Imagine a passenger carrying an open box of buttons. A jolt delivers one knock, a jounce lifts the box, and a lurch sends it sideways. Choose the verb by deciding where the buttons go.
Drill: write the worst ten seconds of the bus ride using three j- words. Then write a hill in one sentence, with one word from the slope scale and no other adjective.
Inventory: the land
The land has thirty names for its ups, its downs and what grows on it. Most of them can be seen from a bus window in an hour.
High ground

rows: a smaller ridge running down from a main one
a steep, rough mass of rock
a long steep face where the land drops
loose stones lying on a slope

blocks.text: Low ground

rows: a wide low area that water drains into
the flat land a river spreads over in flood
wet, spongy ground of rotted plants
a shallow place where a stream can be crossed

blocks.text: What covers it

rows: a row of shrubs and trees between fields
the height above which no trees grow
an open space in a wood

blocks.text: Meander is a river's own name: the Maeander, in what is now Turkey, famous for its loops.
Let a passenger glimpse one landform beyond the glass. One precise sentence can give an otherwise enclosed scene a horizon.
Drill: write the view from the bus in four sentences, with one name from each table and one from the slope scale.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: desultory, insult and salacious, which it marks as probable.

Its page for the root of scandere would not load. The climbing table, the notes on scandal and slander, the other leaping words and the land names are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Stretching and Folding, and the Bed
lessons.label: Week 14

blocks.text: Week 14: Stretching and Folding, and the Bed

Week 14 pairs verbs 27 and 28 (stretch and fold) with the str- family for long, thin things. Practice the words for folds, a scale for tension, and thirty names for a bed and its parts. Begin each session with last week’s slope scale and cover the answer column.
Verbs 27 and 28: stretch and fold
These are the verbs for what a hand does to cloth, and Latin built its words for attention and for meaning out of them. To attend is to stretch toward; to explain is to unfold.
27. tendere, tens- or tent-: to stretch

rows: to stretch in front, as a cover
to stretch forward, as an omen
to hold out, as an offer

blocks.text: Same root: week 1's tenere, to hold, is the same stretching, kept up. So are tenuous and tendon, and Greek tone: the stretch of a string.
Cousin: thin. A thin thing is a stretched one.
Awake: She gave him her attention: stretched her whole mind toward him, like a hand held out across a table.
In the books:

rows: The red light of the setting sun seemed to have a portentous meaning, with which the alarming bray of the second donkey with the log on its foot must surely have some connection.
G. Eliot, The Mill on the Floss (1860), I.11
A portent is a sign stretched out ahead. Maggie reads omens into a donkey's bray.
The ostensible reason why Ahab did not go on board of the whaler we had spoken was this: the wind and sea betokened storms.
Ostensible, held out to be seen. The shown reason sends us looking for the hidden one.
“You’ll stay here a minute,” said he, in a deep, brutal voice, while his nostrils distended and his eye shot a spark of sinister fire.
C. Brontë, The Professor (1857), ch. V
Distend, to stretch apart. The anger shows in the nostrils before the threat is finished.
This warmer light mingles itself with the cold spirituality of the moonbeams, and communicates, as it were, a heart and sensibilities of human tenderness to the forms which fancy summons up.
Tender, stretched thin and so easily touched. Firelight gives moonlit things a heart.
The paint on the front pillars became streaky; the white ball was knocked off the left-hand door-post; the green blinds darkened, then lost all pretense of color.
Fitzgerald, "The Lees of Happiness", in Tales of the Jazz Age (1922)
Pretense, what is held out in front. The house stops even claiming a colour.

blocks.text: 28. plicare, plicat-: to fold
Its partner plectere, plex-, means to braid, and the two families are mixed.

rows: to fold in, to involve in work

blocks.text: Worn down: ply, pliant, plait, pleat (week 6) and splay, which is display cut short. Supple may belong here too, as "folding under".
Cousin: flax, the plant you plait.
Awake: He made the matter explicit: unfolded it on the table, crease by crease, until nothing was underneath.
In the books:

rows: Of one not easily jealous, but, being wrought, / Perplex'd in the extreme…
Perplexed, folded through and through, tangled past undoing. Othello asks to be remembered this way.
I knew as well that he could mould her pliant nature into any form he chose, as I know, now, that he did it.
Pliant, easily folded. The child watches Murdstone shape his mother like clay.
For Ricardo was sincere in his indignation before the elementary principle of loyalty to a chum violated in cold blood, slowly, in a patient duplicity of years.
Duplicity, a twofold folding. A patient duplicity of years makes betrayal a long craft.
Natasha rose slowly and carefully, crossed herself, and stepped cautiously on the cold and dirty floor with her slim, supple, bare feet.
Tolstoy, War and Peace, tr. Louise and Aylmer Maude (1922), XI.31
Supple, bending under. Three adjectives, then bare feet on a cold floor.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take intend, pretend, imply and reply. Use each so that something is stretched or folded.
Long thin things: the str- family
English stretches its long, narrow, pulled things under str-. Street is not one of them; it belongs to next week's verb.

rows: one thread of a rope, or one hair
a long narrow band of color

blocks.text: What cloth does: folds

rows: keeps the line of a fold
is pressed into small regular folds
draws up into small tight wrinkles

blocks.text: A scale for tension
From least pull to most: slack, loose, snug, taut, tight, strained, rigid.

Picture three sheets in a laundry basket. One has bunched up in ridges, another is generally rumpled, and a third has a sharp crease from being folded. Choose rucked, rumpled or creased to match the shape you see.
Drill: describe a set of bedclothes just after it is laid out and again the next morning. Use two fold words in each description and one word from the tension scale.
Inventory: the bed

The word bed can name very different objects. Week 2 introduced the pillow and Week 6 the cloth. Use this inventory of thirty words to distinguish the frame, the layers of bedding and the kind of bed.
The frame

rows: the upright board at the head
the long board down each side
one of the crosswise boards that carry the mattress
the ornament on top of a post
a small wheel under a leg
the sprung base under a mattress
a cloth roof hung over a bed

blocks.text: The bedding

rows: the thin layer between mattress and sheet
a tight folded corner, tucked like an envelope
a thick soft quilt used inside a cover
two layers of cloth stitched over padding
an old word for a bedspread
the skirt that hides the space under a bed

blocks.text: Kinds of bed

rows: a bed built in a tier
a low bed that rolls under another
a couch that serves as a bed
a mattress that folds into a seat
a hanging bed of net or cloth
a thin mattress on the floor
a bed on a ship or a train

blocks.text: A pallet was first a bed of straw; the word is French for straw, made small.
A boarding-house cot, a futon and a four-poster suggest different lives. Try each noun in the same sentence and ask which details a reader can now infer.
Drill: describe a bed in three sentences. Identify one part of its frame, one piece of bedding and the kind of bed it is.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots ten- and plek-, which list the words in the two verb tables with tone, thin, flax and splay.

The plek- page does not list supple or simple, so supple is hedged here and simple is left out. The glosses, the note on pallet and the bed names are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Building and Ruin, and the Toolbox
lessons.label: Week 15

blocks.text: Week 15: Building and Ruin, and the Toolbox

Week 15 is verbs 29 and 30 (loosen, build), a palette for ruin, a scale for coming apart, and thirty names from the toolbox and the joints it makes. Start each session with last week's fold table, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 29 and 30: loosen and build
These two are opposites: one takes things apart, the other piles them up. Between them they hold the words for solving, dissolving, constructing and destroying.
29. solvere, solut-: to loosen
The verb is itself a compound: se-, apart, on luere, to loose.

rows: to loosen a knot, or a problem
to loosen back into its parts; to settle
able to loosen a debt, or a substance

blocks.text: Greek cousin: lyein, to loosen, gives analysis (a loosening up), paralysis (a loosening beside) and catalyst.
English cousins: loose, lose, loss, forlorn and the ending -less.
Awake: The sugar did not vanish. It was dissolved: loosened grain from grain, until the water held all of it.
In the books:

rows: O that this too too solid flesh would melt, / Thaw, and resolve itself into a dew!
Resolve in its root sense, to loosen back. Melt, thaw, resolve, dew: four steps down to water.

The cloud-capp'd towers, the gorgeous palaces, / The solemn temples, the great globe itself, / Yea, all which it inherit, shall dissolve, / And, like this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind.
The whole world loosened like a cloud. Insubstantial is week 10's stare: nothing standing under it.
He watched it, then dropped another daisy into the water, and after that another, and sat watching them with bright, absolved eyes, crouching near on the bank.
Lawrence, Women in Love (1920), ch. XI
Absolved, loosened from guilt. The eyes have been let go.
His eyes, dark brown and quick-shifting, were dissolute.
Dissolute, loosened apart. One plain sentence that ends on its verdict.
Forlorn! the very word is like a bell / To toll me back from thee to my sole self!
An English cousin of solvere, from the root for loss. Keats hears the word itself as a bell.

blocks.text: 30. struere, struct-: to pile up, to build

rows: what is built beneath, or above

blocks.text: Cousins: the ancient root meant to spread. It gives strew, straw (what is strewn) and street, which is via strata: a road paved by spreading.
Stratus, the cloud of week 8, and prostrate, the posture of week 10, are traced to the same root. So is consternation: being laid flat.
Awake: Grief did not destroy the house. It un-built it, taking down in a month what forty years had piled up.
In the books:

rows: But men may construe things after their fashion, / Clean from the purpose of the things themselves.
Construe, to build together. Cicero warns that people build meanings the facts will not bear.
To me, he was in reality become no longer flesh, but marble; his eye was a cold, bright, blue gem; his tongue a speaking instrument—nothing more.
C. Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847), ch. XXXV
Instrument, a thing built for use. St John Rivers is reduced to his tools.
The boatswain, with one leg and one arm embracing a stanchion, struggled with a lamp pressed to his breast, trying to get a light, and growling all the time like an industrious gorilla.
Industry, building within: diligence. The adjective belongs to a clerk, the noun to an ape.
They could not understand; and suddenly the calm sea, the sky without a cloud, appeared formidably insecure in their immobility, as if poised on the brow of yawning destruction.
Destruction, un-building. Poised, from week 1's pendere, holds the calm on the edge before the fall.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take resolve, absolute, instruct and obstruct. Use each so that something comes loose or goes up.
A palette for ruin
Fiction lives in used places, and English is rich in words for how things wear out. Cover the right-hand column.

rows: the soft sheen that age gives a surface
the green crust on old copper
grey-white growth on damp cloth or a wall
furry growth on old food or wet wood
a surface coming off in small thin pieces
bent out of true by damp or heat
loose in the joints, likely to fall
badly made, about to come apart
worn by sun, wind and rain

blocks.text: Dilapidated has stone in it: Latin lapis. The word first meant to scatter like stones.
Coming apart, and piling up

rows: chip, crack, split, crumble, cave in, collapse

blocks.text: A warped plank has been bent out of shape, often by damp. Try the verb in a different setting: an uneven pane warps the lettering on a shop across the street. What suggestion of damage travels with the verb?
Drill: describe a worn object in a room with three words from the palette. Convey age through what has happened to its surface or shape, without naming its age.
Inventory: the toolbox and the joint
Making things has thirty names that most people point at. A character who knows them is a different person from one who does not.
Tools

rows: the forked back of a hammer head, for pulling nails
the rounded back of some hammer heads
the handle of a hammer or an axe
a tool that shaves wood smooth
a bench clamp with two jaws
the tool with a bubble that finds flat
a weight on a string that finds straight down
the L-shaped tool for right angles
a thin wedge that fills a gap
a trestle to rest wood on while sawing

blocks.text: Cuts and joints

rows: an edge cut at a slant
a small flat cut along a corner
two ends cut at an angle to meet in a corner
the hole cut to take a tongue
fan-shaped fingers that lock two boards
a step cut along an edge

blocks.text: Fixings

rows: a hole that lets a screw head sit below the surface
a small hole drilled first, to guide a screw
a flat ring under a nut
a nut with two wings, turned by hand
the spiral ridge of a screw
the smooth part of a screw below its head

blocks.text: Plumb is Latin for lead, the weight on the line. A plumber worked in lead, and aplomb is standing by the plumb line: upright and balanced.
A cabinetmaker asks for a plumb line; a volunteer brings a spirit level. Write their next exchange. What can you tell about each person from the terms they use?
Drill: write a character fixing one small thing in 150 words, with four names from the tables and no explanation of any.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots leu- and stere-, and for dilapidate and aplomb.

The stere- page lists industry, straw, street, stratus, prostrate and consternation. The glosses, the note on plumber and the tool names are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Shutting and Joining, and the Fastening
lessons.label: Week 16

blocks.text: Week 16: Shutting and Joining, and the Fastening

Week 16 is verbs 31 and 32 (shut, join), the kn- family for knots and knobs, the verbs for closing and joining, and thirty names from locks, hinges and fastenings. Start each session with last week's ruin palette, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 31 and 32: shut and join
These are the verbs of the door and the knot. Latin's word for a key and its word for a nail belong with the first, and the yoke belongs to the second.
31. claudere, claus-: to shut
In compounds the stem becomes -clude and -clus-.

rows: to shut beforehand, to rule out
a closing: of a sentence, of a contract

blocks.text: Worn down: close and closure.

The key and the nail: Latin clavis and clavus are traced to the same root. They give clavicle ("little key", in week 4), conclave (a room with a key), enclave (keyed in), clef (a key in music) and clove, the spice shaped like a nail.
Awake: The meeting concluded: its doors shut together, and what had not been said stayed inside.
In the books:

rows: There's something in his soul / O'er which his melancholy sits on brood; / And I do doubt the hatch and the disclose / Will be some danger…
Disclose as a noun: the shell un-shutting at the hatch. Claudius pictures Hamlet's grief as an egg.

I had, in this closet, a field- bed and a hammock, hung from the ceiling, two chairs and a table, neatly screwed to the floor, to prevent being tossed about by the agitation of the horse or the coach.
A closet is a small shut room. Gulliver's is a box carried on horseback, furnished down to the screws.

On the doorsteps there were lounging footmen with bright parti-coloured plumage and white polls, like an extinct race of monstrous birds; and butlers, solitary men of recluse demeanour, each of whom appeared distrustful of all other butlers.
Recluse, shut away. The hermit's word goes to butlers, and the joke turns on itself.
Old Mrs. Varnum, by this time, had gone up to bed, and her daughter and I were sitting alone, after supper, in the austere seclusion of the horse- hair parlour.
Seclusion, shut apart. Austere and horse-hair give it a texture you can feel.

blocks.text: 32. jungere, junct-: to join

rows: to join on, as a duty
to come together, in a charge

blocks.text: Cousins: yoke in English, yoga in Sanskrit ("union") and zeugma in Greek ("a yoking"). Jugular means "of the yoke": the collarbone, and so the neck.
Awake: She closed the door and the subject. That is a zeugma: two things yoked to one verb.
In the books:

rows: The time is out of joint. O cursed spite / That ever I was born to set it right!
Time as a dislocated bone, and Hamlet the one who must set it. Spite is week 1's specere.
This happened at a juncture when Themistocleus had bitten Alkid on the ear, and the said Alkid, with frowning eyes and open mouth, was preparing himself to sob in piteous fashion…
Gogol, Dead Souls, tr. D. J. Hogarth (1915), I.2
Juncture, a joining point in time. The grand word marks a children's fight.
When Phoebe awoke,— which she did with the early twittering of the conjugal couple of robins in the pear-tree,—she heard movements below stairs…
Hawthorne, The House of the Seven Gables (1851)
Conjugal, yoked together. A marriage word for two birds makes the morning domestic.
Her heart was so black and tangled in the teaching, her personal self was shut in prison, abolished, she was subjugate to a bad, destructive will.
Subjugate as an adjective, under the yoke. Shut in prison, abolished, subjugate: the clauses tighten.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take include, preclude, adjoin and juxtapose. Use each so that something shuts or meets.
Knots and knobs: the kn- family
English keeps its knobby, knotted, compact things under kn-. The k was once spoken, as it still is in German.

rows: a tie in a cord; a hard lump in wood
a small ridge cut for grip

blocks.text: Shutting and joining

rows: shutting a door, softest to hardest
ease shut, close, shut, latch, bolt, lock, bar, seal
the sound it makes, softest to hardest

blocks.text: Joining has a verb for each method.

rows: How two things are made one
with cord wound round and round
by weaving two rope ends together
How two things are made one

blocks.text: Picture two parcels being closed. A metal clasp clicks; a paper tab may barely make a sound. Let the verb suggest both the force of the hand and what a listener would hear.
Drill: write a door being shut by three different people, with three verbs and three sounds.
Inventory: fastenings
The things that hold other things shut have thirty names, from a hinge to a zipper. Your pockets and your front door carry most of them.
The door

rows: the jointed plate a door swings on
the rod that holds a hinge together
the bar through the door that the knobs turn
the sprung tongue that holds a door shut
the metal plate on the frame that receives it
the heavy bolt thrown by a key
the short chain that lets a door open a hand's width

blocks.text: Lock and key

rows: the hinged strap a padlock closes
the loop the hasp fits over
a pin inside a lock that the key must lift
the part of a key you hold
the part that enters the lock
a ridge inside a lock that stops the wrong key

blocks.text: On clothes and gear

rows: a frame with a pin, for a belt or a strap
a small catch that holds two ends
a short bar pushed through a loop
a small hook and its loop
the slit a button goes through
the part of a zipper that travels
the tag you pull it by
a metal ring that lines a hole
a fitting that a rope is tied off to

blocks.text: An escutcheon is a shield: Latin scutum.

Compare a keyed fastening with a magnetic cabinet catch. The former gives you words such as ward, tumbler and bit; the catch has a magnet and a plate. Changing the mechanism changes which words the ending can use.
Drill: write someone locking up for the night in five sentences, with five names and one sound from the scale above.
Sources

Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots klau- and yeug-, which list the words in the two verb tables with clavicle, conclave, enclave, clef, clove, yoke, yoga, zeugma, jugular, adjust and joust.
The glosses, the note on escutcheon and the names of the fastenings are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Clinging and Breathing, and the Tree
lessons.label: Week 17

blocks.text: Week 17: Clinging and Breathing, and the Tree

Week 17 is verbs 33 and 34 (stick, breathe), a second cl- family for holding fast, a palette for stickiness, a scale for breath, and thirty names from a tree. Start each session with last week's joining verbs, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 33 and 34: stick and breathe
One of these is the smallest family in the kit and the other is among the largest. To stick gives a handful of words; to breathe gives the words for plotting, sweating, hoping and dying.
33. haerere, haes-: to stick

rows: to stick in, to belong by nature

blocks.text: Latin had a second sticking word, gluten, which gives glue, gluten and glutinous.
Awake: She hesitated: stuck fast in the doorway, as if the air there were thicker.
In the books:

rows: Nor time nor place / Did then adhere, and yet you would make both.
Adhere, to stick together. Time and place did not fit, so Macbeth would make them fit.
In the old oak-wood a mist was rising, and he hesitated, wondering whether one whiteness were a strand of fog or only campion-flowers pallid in a cloud.
Hesitate, to stick fast. He stops between two whites, and the sentence stops with him.
He sat down in one of the armchairs; the big dark dining table twinkled here and there in the small candle-light; the pictures on the wall, all of them very brown, looked vague and incoherent.
H. James, The Portrait of a Lady (1881), ch. XV
Incoherent, not sticking together. In candlelight the pictures come apart.
…whilst their heads and shoulders were still enjoying day, touched with a yellow of self- sustained brilliancy that seemed inherent rather than acquired.
Hardy, Far from the Madding Crowd (1874), ch. XXIII
Inherent, sticking in: light that seems to belong to the shearers. Self-sustained is week 1's tenere.

blocks.text: 34. spirare, spirat-: to breathe

rows: to breathe out, for the last time
to breathe toward, to long for
to breathe across; then, to leak out

blocks.text: Worn down: sprite and sprightly, which are spirit said fast.
Sister words: Latin anima, breath, gives animal and animate. Greek psyche and pneuma both mean breath, and give psychology and pneumonia.
A tree transpires: it breathes water out through its leaves. That is why this week's inventory is a tree.
Awake: They conspired without a word: breathed together in the dark until they were one animal.
In the books:

rows: The candle, wasted at last, went out; as it expired, I perceived streaks of grey light edging the window curtains: dawn was then approaching.
C. Brontë, Jane Eyre (1847), ch. XX
Expire, to breathe out. The candle dies with a breath, and the dawn arrives in the same sentence.
Not so in deserts where the grand / The wild—the terrible conspire / With their own breath to fan his fire.
Conspire, to breathe together, and Poe spells it out: with their own breath.

There were a hundred thousand shapes and substances of incompleteness, wildly mingled out of their places, upside down, burrowing in the earth, aspiring in the air, mouldering in the water, and unintelligible as any dream.
Aspire, to breathe toward. The railway rubble climbs into the air between burrowing and mouldering.
All memorable events, I should say, transpire in morning time and in a morning atmosphere.
Transpire, to breathe through. Events breathe out of the morning like mist.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take adhere, inherent, inspire and expire. Use each so that something sticks or breathes.
Holding fast: a second cl- family
Week 2 gave cl- to hard sounds: click, clack, clang. The same letters hold another family, for things that grip or stick together.

rows: closes tight, of a hand or teeth
a vise, a hand on an arm
fastens two ends with a catch
holds on and will not let go
a child, wet cloth, a smell
a nail bent over, a deal
a tongue to the roof of the mouth

blocks.text: Cleave is two verbs with one spelling. One means to cling, the other to split, and they are opposites.
A palette for stickiness

rows: it holds to whatever touches it
stretchy and sticky, like chewed gum
smooth and faintly sticky, like a candle

blocks.text: Week 6 has tacky and clammy, which belong here too.
A scale for breath
From quietest to most labored: breathe, sigh, puff, huff, pant, gasp, wheeze, rasp, choke.
Breath has its own sound in English: bl-. Blow, blast, bloat, blister and bladder all blow or swell.
Give a character one audible or visible breath during a scene. A small change in breathing can keep a body present through a paragraph of thought.
Drill: describe breathing at three moments: before a race, at the starting signal, and just beyond the finish line. Choose a different word from the scale for each moment.
Inventory: the tree
A tree has thirty names from its root to its seed, and most stories have a tree somewhere in view. Find a real one and work down the tables with it in front of you.
Trunk and wood

rows: the trunk below the first branches
the thin growing layer under the bark
the pale living wood under that
the fork where a branch leaves the trunk
the widening where trunk meets ground

blocks.text: Branch and leaf

rows: a leaf or flower before it opens
the point on a stem where a leaf grows
one of the smaller branching lines
the smaller trees and shrubs beneath
the fallen leaves on the ground

blocks.text: Seed and sap

rows: the juice that rises in a tree
the sticky gum of pines and firs
a hanging tassel of tiny flowers
the woody seed case of a pine
a winged seed, as of a maple
the fallen nuts of forest trees, as food for animals

blocks.text: A twig with tight buds dates a scene differently from a branch heavy with seed. Give a nearby tree one named part that lets the reader infer the season.
Drill: describe a tree at dusk in four sentences, with one name from each table and one word from the sticky palette.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: hesitate, for haerere and its "stick fast, stammer".
The rest of this tab is given from memory: the two verb tables, the notes on gluten, sprite, anima and cleave, and the tree names. Look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Writing and Placing, and the Book
lessons.label: Week 18

blocks.text: Week 18: Writing and Placing, and the Book

Week 18 is verbs 35 and 36 (write, put), a palette for marks and stains, the verbs for putting a thing down, and thirty names from a book, its page and its letters. Start each session with last week's breath scale, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 35 and 36: write and put
These are the writer's own verbs: making a mark and setting a thing down. The first began as cutting or scratching, and the second has a famous set of false friends.
35. scribere, script-: to write

rows: to write down, to picture in words
to write beforehand, as an order
to write up publicly, as an outlaw
to write around, to draw a limit

blocks.text: Standing alone: scribe, script, scripture, scribble.
Worn down: scrivener, and shrive and shrift. English borrowed the verb early for what a priest did: he prescribed a penance. A short shrift was a quick confession before a hanging.
Awake: The doctor prescribed: wrote the order first and let the body follow it.
In the books:

rows: Make a short shrift; he longs to see your head.
Where short shrift comes from: a quick confession before an execution.
"Yes—I know," Selden assented curtly, turning back into the room, but only to stir about with restless steps in the circumscribed space between door and window.
Wharton, The House of Mirth (1905), I.8
Circumscribed, a line written round. The small room is all the freedom he has.
He saw this with his intellectual eye, just for a short fleeting while, as by the light of a falling lamp one might momentarily see an inscription on a wall before being enshrouded in darkness.
An inscription is writing cut in. Hardy shows it for one moment in falling light.
I should have stated before that ground glass folding-doors divided my premises into two parts, one of which was occupied by my scriveners, the other by myself.
A scrivener is a copyist, a man whose job is writing. The doors divide the office as the story will.

blocks.text: 36. ponere, posit-: to put

rows: a putting; where a thing is put
a word put before a noun
one put in front, in charge
a way of placing the body
one who puts on a false face
a place where things are put back

blocks.text: False friends: pose, compose, depose, impose and propose are a different verb. They came through French poser from Late Latin pausare, to pause, which took over ponere's meanings.
Awake: She postponed the letter: put it after supper, then after sleep, then after everything.
In the books:

rows: Out of the eater came forth meat, and out of the strong came forth sweetness. And they could not in three days expound the riddle.
Expound, to set out. The riddle is so short that no one can lay it open.

She writhed into some new posture constantly: stiffening her arms, twisting them before her face, as though to shut out from her eyes the little light there was, and drooping her head, as if it were heavy with insupportable recollections.
Posture, a placing of the body. Writhed, from vertere, and three participles keep re- placing it.
She looked a good deal older, but her eye was as bright as ever and her head as erect; her thin lips seemed a repository of latent meanings.
H. James, The Portrait of a Lady (1881), ch. LIV
A repository is a place where things are put away. The lips store what they will not say.
The machine was painted in bright hues of green, yellow, and red, and it resembled as a whole a compound of hornet, grasshopper, and shrimp, magnified enormously.
Compound, things put together. Three creatures make one machine.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take describe, subscribe, deposit and opposite. Use each so that a hand writes or sets something down.
A palette for marks
A mark is what one thing leaves on another, and English sorts marks by size and by how they were made. Cover the right-hand column.

rows: a small patch of color or light
a speck of dust in the air
a drop of ink spread on paper
a blurred mark left by rubbing
a mark dragged across a surface
a mark that has soaked in
a rough dab of paint or mud
a mark from a shoe or a knock
a small cut in an edge
a hollow knocked into a surface
the mark of a healed wound

blocks.text: The sm- words are the dirty ones: smear, smudge, smut, smirch, smoke, smolder.
Putting down, and writing down

rows: set, lay, place, rest, prop, lodge, wedge, plant, plunk, plop, drop, dump
jot, scribble, dash off, pen, print, inscribe, engrave

blocks.text: The verb you choose for putting a cup on a table tells the reader the mood of the hand. Set is careful; plunk is not.
Lift a thumb from a glossy dust jacket. Is the mark a clear print, a smudge or a smear? Choose the word that shows how the hand moved.
Drill: write one character putting down five objects in five moods, with five verbs from the scale.
Inventory: the book
The thing you are trying to make has thirty names of its own. Take a hardcover off the shelf and find them.
The book

rows: the back edge, where the pages are bound
the stiff front or back of a hardcover
the sheet glued inside the cover
the blank leaf at the front or the back
the picture facing the title page
the page that gives title, author and publisher
the note that says how and where the book was made
a folded section of pages, sewn as one
the small cloth band at the top of the spine

blocks.text: The page

rows: a left-hand page; the back of a leaf
the inner margin, where two pages meet
the line of title at the top of each page
a paragraph's last line, stranded at the top of a page
a paragraph's first line, stranded at the bottom
a large first letter that hangs down several lines

blocks.text: The letter

rows: the small foot at the end of a stroke
the part of b or d that rises above the small letters
the tail of p or g that hangs below the line
the line the letters sit on
the height of a small x
the enclosed space in o or e
two letters joined as one, like fi
adjusting the space between two letters

blocks.text: Leading is said "ledding": printers spaced their lines with strips of lead. Upper case and lower case were the two trays the metal letters were kept in.
The white space that week 9 of the fiction course uses is, to a printer, leading, margin and gutter.
Drill: find ten of these names in a book you love. Then write one sentence on how its page looks, using three of them.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its page for the root skribh-, which lists every scribere word here with shrive and shrift, and its page for pose, for the false friends.
The ponere table, the notes on short shrift, leading and the type cases, and the names of the book's parts are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.
Week 19: Moving, and the Body

Week 19 is verbs 37 and 38 (move, drive), a scale for trembling, the verbs for moving a thing, and thirty names from the body below the neck. Start each session with last week's marks palette, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 37 and 38: move and drive
These two are the engine verbs: one moves, the other makes things move. Emotion, motive and moment come from the first; act, exact and essay come from the second.
37. movere, mot-: to move

rows: what moves a person, or a story
a moving out, of the mind

blocks.text: Worn down: mob and mutiny. Mob is the Latin phrase mobile vulgus, "the fickle crowd", cut down to its first syllable.
Awake: The emotion was a motion first: something moved out of her chest before she had a name for it.
In the books:

rows: Thou on whose stream, mid the steep sky's commotion, / Loose clouds like earth's decaying leaves are shed…
P. B. Shelley, "Ode to the West Wind" (1820)
Commotion, a moving together. Decaying is week 8's cadere.
The flame retreats to some remote and platonic fire; the white heat has gone from the iron and the glow from the coal.
Fitzgerald, The Beautiful and Damned (1922), bk. I
Remote, moved back. The flame withdraws in the first clause, and the second shows what it left.
Yalta was hardly visible through the morning mist; white clouds stood motionless on the mountain-tops.
Chekhov, "The Lady with the Dog", tr. Constance Garnett (1917), II
The clouds do not move, so the two people beneath them can be still.
It was falling on every part of the dark central plain, on the treeless hills, falling softly upon the Bog of Allen and, farther westward, softly falling into the dark mutinous Shannon waves.
Mutinous, moving against. The one restless word in a sentence of soft falling.
Without a tremor in her voice, or frame, and passing onward with a foot that set itself upon the neck of every soft emotion, she bade her mother good-night, and repaired to her own room.
Emotion, a moving out. Edith treads on each one as it rises.

blocks.text: 38. agere, act-: to drive, to do

rows: a turning over together, in the mind
driven out; weighed to the grain

blocks.text: Worn down: cache, and squat, which is "pressed together": week 10's posture.
Greek cousin: agein, to lead, gives agony (a contest), pedagogue ("child-leader"), demagogue, synagogue and strategy ("army-leading").
Awake: The evidence was cogent: it drove every doubt into one corner and shut the gate.
In the books:

rows: O limed soul, that, struggling to be free, / Art more engag'd! Help, angels! Make assay.
Assay, a trial. Claudius asks the angels to make the attempt he cannot.
His face was not as square as his son's, and, indeed, the chin, though firm enough in outline, retreated a little, and the lips, ambiguous, were curtained by a moustache.
Ambiguous, driving both ways. The lips are set off by commas and then hidden.
To burn the bones of the king of Edom for lime, seems no irrational ferity; but to drink of the ashes of dead relations, a passionate prodigality.
T. Browne, Hydriotaphia, Urn- Burial (1658), ch. III
Prodigal, driving forth, spending. Browne weighs two barbarities in balanced clauses.
The sun had set behind a bank of cloud, and only a faint yellow light was giving its farewell kisses to the waves, which were agitated by an active breeze.
Agitate, to drive to and fro. The waves are already moving before anything happens on them.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take remote, moment, agent and exact. Use each so that something moves or is driven.
A scale for trembling
A body that shakes is telling the reader why, if you pick the right word. The scale runs from the slightest movement to the most violent.

rows: a lip, a leaf, held-back feeling
a quick shaking that comes in waves
one strong shake through the whole body
the plain word for all of it
a deep shaking of something large
violent shaking that cannot be stopped

blocks.text: Single movements have their own words: twitch (one small muscle), flinch (away from a blow), wince (at a pain), start (at a surprise).
Moving a thing
Shake, shiver, shudder, shimmy, shift, shuffle and shrug all begin alike. English gives sh- to small restless movements.
Let a sensation produce a visible action. A character with a cramped calf might wince, flinch or hold a breath. Choose one movement a bystander could see.
Drill: describe a character at the sharpest moment of a cramp in three sentences. Include one word from the trembling scale and one distinct single movement.
Inventory: the body
Week 4 named the face and the hand; this week names the rest, in thirty names from the shoulder to the ball of the foot. Week 14 of the fiction course needs every one of them.
The trunk

rows: the flat bone at the back of the shoulder
the flat bone down the middle of the chest
the column of bones down the back
the inward curve above the hips, at the back
the front of the body between chest and waist
the scar where the cord was cut
the fold where thigh meets body
the jut of bone at the side, below the waist
the last bones of the spine

blocks.text: The arm

rows: the muscle at the front of the upper arm
the inside of the bent elbow
the spot at the elbow that tingles when knocked
the arm from elbow to wrist
the joint of hand and arm
a place where a pulse can be felt

blocks.text: Leg and foot

rows: the tendon at the back of the knee, and the muscle above it
the small bone at the front of the knee
the soft place behind the knee
the front of the lower leg
the muscle at the back of the lower leg
the joint of foot and leg
the cord from calf to heel
the arched upper side of the foot

blocks.text: A muscle is a "little mouse": Latin musculus, for the way one moves under the skin.

Sometimes the inventory names the anatomy, yet the sensation falls between entries. Try describing the spot where a shoe seam rubs a heel. Start with the closest noun, then give the reader the particular location the noun alone cannot convey.
Drill: describe someone at rest in five sentences. Work upward from the feet, using five distinct names from the inventory.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots meue- and ag-, which list the words in the two verb tables with mob, mutiny, motif, cache, squat, essay and the Greek cousins.

The ag- page lists agitation and cogitation, not the verbs, so the table uses the nouns. The glosses, the note on muscle and the body names are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.

lessons.title: Making and Seeing, and the Colors
lessons.label: Week 20

blocks.text: Week 20: Making and Seeing, and the Colors

Week 20 is the last two verbs (make, see), a palette for how a color behaves, the verbs for showing and hiding, and thirty exact colors with what each was named for. Start each session with last week's trembling scale, right-hand column covered.
Verbs 39 and 40: make and see
The last two verbs are among the largest families in Latin, and they are the two acts a writer performs: to make a thing, and to see it. Revision is in here, and so is story.
39. facere, fact-: to make, to do
In compounds the stem becomes -fic- and -fect-, and at the end of a verb it becomes -fy.
Worn down: feat, feature, fashion, profit, affair ("to do"), defeat (un-done), counterfeit (made against the original), surfeit (overdone) and fetish: a made thing, a charm.
Cousins: do, deed, deem and doom in English. In Greek, thesis and theme: a thing set down.
Awake: He was defeated in the exact sense: undone, like a knot.
In the books:

rows: Shake off this downy sleep, death's counterfeit, / And look on death itself!
Counterfeit, made against an original: sleep is death's copy.
…Upon whose property and most dear life / A damn'd defeat was made.
Defeat, an undoing. The king was not beaten; he was undone.
…he shook his head, laughing, rose and bid her good-morning, with courtesy, but still with the regardless air of one whom too much unsolicited attention was surfeiting and spoiling.
Surfeit, overdone. Too much attention works like too much food.

It was a bare, resounding room smelling of stables, with cane forms along the walls, and the walls ornamented at regular intervals with painted lyres and little cut-glass branches for candles, which seemed to be shedding their old- fashioned drops as other branches might shed autumn leaves.
Fashion is a making. The candle branches become trees, and their glass drops fall like leaves.

blocks.text: 40. videre, vis-: to see
Cousins: wit and wise in English, because to have seen is to know. Guide and guise came in from Germanic. Sanskrit gives Veda.
Greek gives idea, a thing seen. It also gives history and story, from a word for one who knows because he saw.
Awake: She revised him: looked again, and saw what the first look had been in too much of a hurry to see.
In the books:

rows: Despite his aged stoop, Benjamin Button—for it was by this name they called him instead of by the appropriate but invidious Methuselah— was five feet eight inches tall.
Fitzgerald, "The Curious Case of Benjamin Button", in Tales of the Jazz Age (1922)
Invidious, looking against with ill will. The joke sits inside the dashes.
When the sisters came to Willey Water, the lake lay all grey and visionary, stretching into the moist, translucent vista of trees and meadow.
Lawrence, Women in Love (1920), ch. IV
Vista, a view. Visionary and vista, two videre words, frame the lake.
The smoke of the kindled wood rose from the chimney without like a lotus-headed column; local people who were passing by saw it, and thought of the newly- married couple, and envied their happiness.
Hardy, Tess of the d'Urbervilles (1891), ch. XXXVI
Envy, looking at with ill will. The neighbours envy a happiness that has already ended.
She called up before her eyes a vision of the drawing-room at home; it was a large oblong room, with a square window opening on the garden.
Woolf, The Voyage Out (1915), ch. XVI
A vision summoned, then furnished plainly. The plainness is what makes it a memory.

blocks.text: Awake drill: take effect, perfect, evident and revise. Use each so that something is made or seen.
How a color behaves
A color word names a hue. These words say how strong it is, how clean, and what light or time has done to it. Cover the right-hand column.

rows: harsh and unnatural, as under bad light
a dull, unhealthy yellow, of skin
a healthy red, of a face
marked with patches of different shades
marked with spots of light and shade
changing color with the angle of view

blocks.text: Lurid has turned right round. Latin luridus meant pale yellow and ghastly, the color of a bruise, and in English the word first meant pale and wan.
Showing and hiding

rows: veil, mask, cloak, shroud, screen, conceal, obscure, eclipse

blocks.text: To reveal is to draw back a veil; the veil is inside the word.
Look at a room at dusk. Choose one exact color that briefly appears as the daylight fades, then use it to change what the reader notices.
Drill: describe a room’s ceiling at gloaming in two sentences. Use one color from the inventory below and one word from the showing-and-hiding palette.
Inventory: thirty colors
The last inventory is thirty exact colors, each with the thing it was named for. Most color names are stolen from a stone, a plant, an animal or a place.
Reds

rows: What it is, and its namesake
a bright red; first a rich cloth
a deep red; kermes, an insect dye
a bright orange-red; the "little worm" of the same kind of dye
a dark brownish red; French for chestnut
a reddish brown; also a coarse country cloth
a dark purplish brown; French for flea

blocks.text: Yellows and browns

rows: What it is, and its namesake
a clear golden brown; the fossil resin
a yellowish brown; a lion's color
a dark brown; an earth named for shadow, or for Umbria
a reddish brown; the earth of Siena
a warm dark brown; the cuttlefish and its ink
a brownish grey; French for mole

blocks.text: Greens

rows: What it is, and its namesake
a sharp yellow-green; the monks' liqueur

blocks.text: Blues and purples

rows: What it is, and its namesake
a clear sky blue; the stone lapis lazuli
a deep pure blue; "from beyond the sea"
What it is, and its namesake
a pale purple; French for the mallow flower

blocks.text: Pale and dark

rows: What it is, and its namesake
a pale unbleached cream; French for "raw"
a dull yellowish brown; a word for dust
a deep glossy black; a black stone
black, in old and formal use; the fur

blocks.text: Auburn is missing because it changed sides. It first meant whitish, from Latin albus, and turned reddish-brown under the pull of the word brown.
Scarlet and russet were cloths before they were colors, which takes you back to week 6.
Drill: write five sentences about your room, each with one exact color and no other adjective.
After week 20
The kit is complete at forty verbs, and the method is now yours. Here is the stock.

rows: Latin verbs, each with its family

blocks.text: You also have a scale or a palette for light, sound, gait, looking, smell, touch, taste, weather, voice, dark, edges, speed, slope, tension, ruin, joining, breath, marks, trembling and color.
How to keep it
1. Review by covering. One week's tables a day, right-hand column covered, takes ten minutes.
2. Use five a day. Put five words from the kit into whatever fiction you write that day, and cut the ones that show.
3. Build week 21 yourself. Week 10's recipe still holds: two verbs, one sense, one place of thirty names.

Verbs worth building next: legere (to gather, to read), loqui (to speak), sentire (to feel), pati (to suffer), nasci (to be born), vivere (to live), mori (to die), quaerere (to seek), sequi (to follow) and cernere (to sift).
The fiction course ends its twentieth week on your own style. This kit is where that style gets its words.
Sources
Checked against the Online Etymology Dictionary: its pages for the roots dhe- and weid-, and for lurid, auburn, scarlet, crimson, vermilion, puce, umber, sepia, taupe, verdigris and ultramarine.

The dictionary gives both origins for umber and is unsure where scarlet came from. The other twenty-one colors, the glosses in the verb tables and the note on reveal are given from memory; look up any item you plan to rely on in print.
